job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior automation engineer at a food-packaging plant in Santo Vale. I studied mechatronics, and my final project was a small robot arm that sorted fruit by colour. Now I look after the conveyor lines, tune the sensors and write the little programs that tell the packing machines what to do. I use an AI assistant all day to read manuals and draft code. I rent a flat with two colleagues, and on Sundays I go to Mass and then to my mother's for lunch. She sells vegetables at the market and she's very proud of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'm not surprised and not disappointed. It helps me a lot already, but I understand that machines still break and need people. At church people would ask if I'm worried, and I'd say no, not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the plateau is fine, but my wallet isn't. My loan is large and my pay is low, and the plant only has two automation engineers besides me. Santo Vale has hardly any other factories like it, so if the plant slows down I'd have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the plant's controller systems and the AI tools I use every day. I'd save 80 a month, and send 100 to my mother, who needs help with the market stall's rent. And I'd start sketching a small repair workshop for packing machines, just a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about technology, a bit tight about money. I love my work, so I can't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your mother's stall and how you help.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother's stall pays for her rent but not much else. I help when I can, and she'd never ask. That's a promise to myself I'm not going to break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the repair workshop do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The workshop would serve small food producers who can't afford a service contract. There are at least four in the valley. It's not a business yet, but it could be.

At church I'd say I'm not worried about **robots**.
think: The plateau is fine, but my **wallet** isn't, with a big loan and low pay.

feel: I feel **calm** about technology and a bit tight about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and it can be good if people are looked after. At work I'd tell my manager Dorotea that the plant should train operators to work beside the new tools, not replace them. At church I'd say that work is part of dignity, and firms have a duty to the people who built them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is mixed. The programming and manual-reading part is something AI does faster, but the sensors, belts and the fixing still need hands. I'm well placed, but I'm also the newest, and that's a risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for every bit of paperwork and coding, and use the time to take on more of the hands-on tuning. I'd propose to Dorotea that I run a training session for the operators, so they feel part of it. And I'd start the repair workshop on weekends, with two small bakeries as the first customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a stone in my stomach. I like new things, but I'm responsible for my mother, and that makes me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the line are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think about the operators on the line. Many operators on the line are older women who've worked there 20 years. They've got no degree, and I don't know where they would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the plant to promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the plant to promise them retraining before anyone's let go. It's not asking for a lot. It's what you do for people who've given you decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and that I'm worried for ordinary families. At church I'd ask people to look out for each other, and I'd tell my manager that the plant must prepare its people. I wouldn't say I'm panicking, but I'd be loud about a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared, even though I know the tools well. My programming is the first part that goes, and the robots arrive three years later for the rest. I'm 22, with a loan, and a mother who depends on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything I could into savings, maybe 70 percent of my pay, and move into one room in a shared house. I'd push the repair workshop fast, because it's hands-on and local, and the bakeries already trust me. And I'd move my mother's stall rent onto my account, so she has one less worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, but moving. I'd feel better with a to-do list than with sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The workshop could fail. If the two-year clock is true, small food producers might close or buy robots from a supplier. Then I'd have a plan with no customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fallback would be to move to the city, where the factories are bigger. I'd hate leaving my mother, but I'd send money home and visit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time to do things properly. I'd say that firms should train their people and that families should talk about money before the rush. At church I'd say we can help the older ones learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel good, to be honest, cautiously. By 2031 I'd be 27, with years of using AI at depth and a small business behind me. No plan survives meeting real life, so I'd still want savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the workshop to a few regular clients and hire a part-timer in 2029. I'd keep my plant job as the stable base, and aim to clear the loan by 2030. I'd also start a small fund for my mother, 50 a month, so she isn't depending on the stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, like seeing the first light on a long journey. I'd be busy, but happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd watch for is the plant. If the owners suddenly go for full automation in 2029, I'd need to be ready to run the workshop full time. That's the day my plan must be strong enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your mother's advice about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also pray about it, and talk to my mother. She doesn't understand the technology, but she understands people, and her advice is usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift. I'd say people should use it to learn, and firms should use it to invest in their staff. I'd say it at church, at work and anywhere else people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 32 and running a small automation workshop with a few staff. The plant might not need me by then, but if I've built the business, I'd be fine. I'd probably be married, and my mother would be in her own small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the plant job for four years, build the workshop to be my main income and then leave. I'd pay off the loan by 2031 and save for a deposit on a small house in Santo Vale. I'd also train two young people from the town as apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud. Ten years gives me room to build something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking about when you say not everyone is lucky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd worry about is people who are not as lucky. Not everyone has a mother who raised them to be curious, or a manager who lets them learn. I'd want those who don't to have a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentices would be my way of doing something about it. I'd pay them properly, and they'd learn what I learned. That's the thing I'd be proudest of.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I'm quick with the tools. My programming goes first, the robots follow, and I'd have a loan and a mother to support. What would help is paid retraining for the older operators, small business loans and a firm that tells its people early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't think I'm clever to adapt. I had a mother who raised me to be curious and a manager who let me learn. Most people don't get that, and they shouldn't be punished for it.

headlineQuote: I don't think I'm clever to adapt. I had a mother who raised me to be curious and a manager who let me learn.
portrait: Rosa is a **junior automation engineer** at a food-packaging plant, renting a flat with colleagues, and sending money to her market-trader mother.
She is **adaptive** and traditional: uses AI daily, goes to Mass, and plans a repair workshop for small food producers.
Her anxiety is about **family duty** and a loan, not about learning new tools.
She tends to **act early**: saving hard, starting the workshop and speaking up for line operators.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because her programming goes first and her mother and loan depend on her.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining for **older operators**, small business loans and a firm that warns its people early.
